w: What's tested The drug names in each class, above all the ones his slides highlight in red: "Pay attention to those drugs that I highlight in the slides, and you should be fine." The class name gives the mechanism: an aromatase inhibitor inhibits aromatase, "which means that you have to know what aromatase enzyme does" Testosterone's two fates: 5-alpha-reductase makes DHT, the active form, and aromatase makes estradiol; the drugs that block each enzyme, and the man without aromatase who grows tall with weak bones Thromboembolism, "the most serious and most common side effect of estrogens": estrogens raise clotting factors, and the SERMs and aromatase inhibitors share the risk (his raloxifene dental case) The three anti-androgen classes: GnRH analogs (why a long-acting analog switches testosterone off), 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride as Proscar and Propecia) and androgen receptor antagonists The SERMs by use: "tamoxifen for breast cancer, raloxifene for osteoporosis, Clomid... to stimulate ovulation" Testosterone's adverse effects, with hepatotoxicity "the most important", and when to avoid it Emergency contraception: Plan B (levonorgestrel, within 72 hours, no prescription) versus ulipristal (a progestin receptor antagonist, up to 5 days, prescription only) Dr. Pius Fasinu (Pharmacology and Toxicology) gave Lecture 18 on Wednesday, November 11, at 1 pm. His deck, "Pharmacology of Estrogens and Androgens," reviews where the sex steroids come from and what they do, then covers the drugs: the androgens and anti-androgens, the estrogens, the selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs), the aromatase inhibitors, the progestins and the anti-progestins. He worked through five short cases with the class, two of them set in the dental chair. He said he would spend his time on the drugs, since the physiology was covered in your physiology lectures. These notes follow the recording and slides. His objectives: recall the physiologic effects of estrogens and androgens; list examples of estrogenic drugs, SERMs, androgenic drugs and anti-androgenic drugs; discuss the mechanism of each drug class; and highlight their therapeutic uses and safety concerns. His advice: "If you're able to do those, the names will suggest to you how they work, based on their classes." The drugs his slides highlight in red are goserelin, finasteride, dutasteride, flutamide, bicalutamide, tamoxifen, raloxifene, anastrozole, progesterone, hydroxyprogesterone, levonorgestrel and ulipristal. His summary slide adds testosterone, DHEA, estradiol, estrone and ethinyl estradiol. His opening case: testosterone or estrogen? He opened with a quick case: for each condition, which hormone should be avoided, testosterone or estrogen? Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH): avoid testosterone, which fuels prostate enlargement. Breast cancer: avoid estrogen in women, and also testosterone in men. Breast cancer is rare in men, but it happens. A history of thromboembolism (a deep vein clot or a pulmonary embolism): avoid estrogen. "I think it's the most serious and most common side effect of estrogens," he said: estrogens disturb clot formation, so abnormal clotting is typical of estrogen therapy. Pregnancy: testosterone has the most adverse effect. He called it an absolute contraindication in pregnancy. He added that there may be a few instances where estrogen is used in a pregnant woman, but his estrogen slide lists pregnancy as a contraindication to estrogens too. In his case, testosterone is the answer for pregnancy. Where the sex hormones come from His overview chart traces each hormone back to the pituitary: the hypothalamus sends releasing hormones to the anterior pituitary, whose FSH and LH drive the ovaries and testes to make progesterone, estradiol and testosterone. This lecture's hormones are progesterone, testosterone and estrogen, "which is formed from testosterone." The biosynthetic pathway is complex, and his slide is an extract of it. Cholesterol is turned, in several steps, into DHEA, dehydroepiandrosterone, an important precursor. DHEA is converted to androstenedione (or androstenediol) and then to testosterone. DHEAS is the sulfate form of DHEA. His slide's abbreviation table lists DHEA as "dihydrotestosterone." He corrected it in class: DHEA is dehydroepiandrosterone, the precursor; DHT is dihydrotestosterone, the active androgen; DHEAS is the sulfate of DHEA. DHEA matters because it is sold over the counter as a supplement (as prasterone). Many older men take it during andropause, which is like menopause in men, to supplement their testosterone, since it is the precursor of testosterone. It is controversial: every testosterone product is a Schedule III controlled drug except DHEA, which he said has escaped that regulation. Once testosterone is made, it has two fates, and a drug class is built on each. 5-alpha-reductase reduces testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, or DHT. The name tells you what it does: it is a reductase. "Dihydrotestosterone is the active testosterone." Reducing testosterone is its bioactivation, so to lower androgen activity you can give a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor, and no DHT is made. Aromatase aromatizes one of testosterone's rings, turning it into estradiol (and androstenedione into estrone). From estradiol the body can form estrone and estriol. Aromatase inhibitors are popular in treating certain cancers where you don't want estrogenic activity. When there is enough DHT in the body, it feeds back negatively on the hypothalamus and the pituitary. How testosterone is controlled His regulation slide: the hypothalamus releases GnRH (also called LHRH) in a pulsatile way, a short burst and then a long pause. GnRH makes the pituitary release FSH and LH, which drive the testes: they make testosterone and support spermatogenesis. In the target tissues, steroid 5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, which drives male maturation and development and the growth of bone and muscle. Remember the pulses: they explain the GnRH drugs later. What testosterone does He went through the physiological effects quickly, as physiology you have seen: Differentiation of the male fetus from the female, and development of the male reproductive organs before birth and of the secondary sex traits at puberty. Maintenance of reproductive function, mainly sperm formation. It decreases the plasma binding globulins: CBG (corticosteroid-binding globulin), TBG (thyroxine-binding globulin), SHBG (sex hormone-binding globulin) and transferrin. These proteins, made in the liver, carry hormones in the plasma until they reach their target, and a hormone exists in equilibrium between bound and free. Androgens and their analogs lower the plasma levels of these carriers. It increases skin thickness, secretions, pigmentation and circulation. Retention of water and electrolytes, which is why testosterone is not a good drug for people with ongoing cardiovascular problems, including hypertension. It decreases circulating HDL, the good cholesterol, so it is also not good for people with cholesterol problems. It increases protein synthesis and muscle mass, anabolic especially in the upper body. That is why androgens are abused to build muscle in sports, which is not legal and counts as cheating. Erythropoiesis: it increases red blood cell formation, so androgens can treat refractory anemia. Growth: DHT stimulates growth, and estradiol limits it by closing the epiphyses. Increased libido. The growth point is why aromatase deficiency matters. Estradiol is made from testosterone by aromatase, so a man born without aromatase cannot make estradiol, and his epiphyses don't close on time. "They're the ones that grow very tall": long bones, but weak, osteoporotic bones with a high risk of osteoporosis. His slide's treatment is estradiol. How the sex steroids act All the hormones in this block are very lipophilic, and they all bind nuclear receptors: thyroxine, the corticosteroids and the sex steroids alike. In the plasma they travel bound: the sex hormones to sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), while a corticosteroid binds CBG. Only the free hormone reaches the receptor. Testosterone or DHT enters the cell and binds the androgen receptor (DHT is the main ligand, and testosterone binds it too), and the hormone-receptor complex changes gene expression. Because the effect goes through gene transcription, it takes time. Estradiol acts the same way through estrogen receptors. The androgen drugs Testosterone itself is the natural hormone, the standard the others are compared with. It is Schedule III and comes in many forms: IV or depot injection, an implant (Testopel), a buccal tablet (Striant), a nasal gel (Natesto), topical gels (AndroGel, Testim, Vogelxo) and a transdermal patch (Androderm). Testosterone cypionate (Depo-Testosterone) is the one he said is dispensed and injected: an intramuscular depot, released very slowly, injected about once a week or once a month. Testosterone enanthate (Delatestryl) and testosterone undecanoate (Aveed) are other injectable forms. The table's second column compares each drug's androgenic and anabolic activity, because most indications want one or the other. Is the patient deficient in androgenic activity, or do you want anabolic activity, for example for unexplained weight loss with some cancers? Testosterone and its injectable forms are all 1 to 1: the form doesn't change the anabolic activity. For a strongly anabolic drug you would look at the other analogs (fluoxymesterone, oxymetholone, nandrolone, oxandrolone), which are more anabolic than androgenic; oxymetholone and nandrolone also raise red blood cell counts in anemia. He said oxandrolone has been withdrawn. DHEA (prasterone) is on the table as a precursor sold as a supplement, with off-label uses only. What to know from this table, in his words: "You want to know those examples, especially your testosterone standard and the cypionate, which is the depot. I don't think I want to bother you about those other ones." The other analogs are here for reference. Uses and adverse effects of androgens Their mechanism is activation of nuclear androgen receptors. The uses on his slide: Replacement in male hypogonadism, for men who don't produce enough. Some breast tumors in women. Anabolic effects, when clinically indicated. Refractory anemias, through erythropoiesis. Osteoporosis ("not the best drug," he said, but it can be used in women). Growth. Reversing the effects of male aging, andropause. The side effects are more pronounced in women and children, so avoid testosterone in women as much as possible. Women: hirsutism, including facial hair, a deepened voice, an enlarged clitoris and smaller breasts: the changes you expect in boys at puberty. These can be irreversible with prolonged use. Men: sleep apnea ("a big problem"), priapism, increased sex drive, and feminization: gynecomastia and azoospermia. He said the feminization is believed to come from testosterone being converted to estradiol. Both: acne, edema, hepatotoxicity, jaundice, lower HDL and higher LDL, dependence, aggressiveness and psychosis. "I think the most important side effect of testosterone everyone needs to also know is hepatotoxicity." People are screened for it, and a patient who already has a liver problem doesn't get testosterone. A counseling point he gives when dispensing testosterone, especially the cream: apply it last thing at night, before bed. It is lipophilic and passes through the skin very easily (the route is transdermal, not just topical), so if you hug your child after putting it on, the child can get testosterone into their system. The same goes for women. Contraindications and cautions: pregnancy or planning to become pregnant, heart or liver disease, men with prostate or breast cancer, and extreme caution in children (and women). In class he summed it up as pregnancy and liver disease. The anti-androgens: three ways to lower androgen activity "This can be confusing, so often I take time to explain it." An anti-androgen either blocks testosterone at its receptor, prevents its activation to DHT, or shuts down its production. That gives three classes. GnRH analogs The GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) analogs are goserelin (Zoladex), the one he highlighted and one of the most common on the market, leuprolide (Eligard, Lupron), nafarelin (Synarel), triptorelin (Trelstar) and histrelin (Supprelin). The paradox: GnRH should be pro-androgen, because it drives LH and testosterone. The body releases it in pulses, a short burst and then a long pause with no release. These drugs are slow-release, long-acting analogs, so they stimulate the pituitary cells continuously, and eventually the cells switch off: FSH and LH secretion is suppressed, and with it testosterone. "That's the only way it's going to make sense to you": given this way, a GnRH analog works as an anti-androgen. Uses: primarily prostate cancer (what Zoladex is used for), and also benign prostatic hyperplasia, precocious puberty (signs of early puberty), chemical castration and prepubertal cryptorchidism (testes that have not descended). Side effects are mostly anti-sex-hormonal: impotence and gynecomastia, what you expect in hypogonadism. 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors Testosterone is not very active until it is reduced to dihydrotestosterone, so that reduction is its bioactivation. If you don't want androgenic activity, inhibit the enzyme that does it, 5-alpha-reductase. The two he highlighted: finasteride (Proscar, Propecia) and dutasteride (Avodart). Uses: benign prostatic hyperplasia and alopecia. Proscar is important for two reasons: it treats BPH, and a side effect was that it makes people grow hair. So a lower strength was approved for hair loss as Propecia. Proscar and Propecia are the same drug, finasteride: "The difference between Proscar and Propecia is the dose, the strength of the tablet," and the indication. The high strength is for BPH and the low strength for alopecia. (He wasn't sure of the numbers in class; Proscar is 5 mg and Propecia 1 mg.) Side effects: gynecomastia and sexual dysfunction. Androgen receptor antagonists The third class is the one you would naturally think of: drugs that compete with testosterone at its receptor. He highlighted flutamide (Eulexin) and bicalutamide (Casodex); nilutamide (Nilandron) and enzalutamide (Xtandi) are the others on the slide. Mechanism: competitive antagonism of androgen receptors. Uses: prostate cancer in men, and excess androgens in women. Side effects: GI disturbances (least with bicalutamide), gynecomastia and hepatotoxicity. His advice for all three classes: "Try to familiarize with those highlighted examples. That should be enough for you." GnRH analogs Goserelin (Zoladex); also leuprolide (Lupron) Long-acting, continuous stimulation switches off FSH and LH, so testosterone falls Prostate cancer, BPH, precocious puberty, chemical castration Impotence, gynecomastia 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors Finasteride (Proscar, Propecia), dutasteride (Avodart) Block the conversion of testosterone to DHT BPH (higher strength), alopecia (lower strength) Gynecomastia, sexual dysfunction Androgen receptor antagonists Flutamide (Eulexin), bicalutamide (Casodex) Compete with testosterone at the androgen receptor Prostate cancer; excess androgens in women GI disturbances (least with bicalutamide), gynecomastia, hepatotoxicity His Case 2: which enzyme activates testosterone? Which enzyme converts circulating testosterone to its biologically active form? Ask whether you need to aromatize or to reduce. The active form, dihydrotestosterone, is a reduced testosterone, so the answer is 5-alpha-reductase. For testosterone to estradiol, it would be aromatase: "When you aromatize the ring, it becomes estrogen." The natural estrogens There are three natural estrogens: Estradiol (E2), made in the ovary: the main estrogen. Estrone (E1), made in the liver and peripheral tissues. Estriol (E3), also made in the liver and peripheral tissues. When aromatase converts testosterone you get estradiol (and from androstenedione, estrone), and these two can be converted to estriol. Estrone and estriol are conjugated and secreted into the bile, then reactivated and reabsorbed in the gut: enterohepatic recirculation. Oral estrogens have more effects on the liver, including an increase in clotting factors. The mechanism is like the androgens'. In plasma, estrogen is in equilibrium between free and bound to SHBG and albumin. Free estrogen binds the estrogen receptor, found in the cytoplasm and the nucleus. A receptor bound in the cytoplasm moves into the nucleus, where the complex alters gene expression. What estrogen does Female maturation: development of the vagina, uterus and secondary sex traits. Endometrium: growth of the uterine muscle and development of the uterine lining. Metabolic: estrogen increases HDL, unlike testosterone, which lowers it, and it increases triglycerides, with a slight increase in LDL on his slide. Because of the triglycerides, he said, estrogens are not good for people with cardiovascular issues. It maintains the skin and blood vessels in women. That is why doctors sometimes prescribe oral contraceptives to teenagers, even in high school: not for contraception, but for very bad skin as they approach puberty. It antagonizes PTH-mediated bone calcium resorption, which protects bone. Coagulation: it increases production of clotting factors 2, 7, 9 and 10 and decreases antithrombin III. That last point is the one he kept coming back to: "Drugs that are estrogenic, even those that are anti-estrogenic, they tend to increase clotting factors, and that's why they have a problem with thrombosis": pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis and other clots. His second slide of effects adds an increase in progesterone receptor synthesis and in libido, then a list he skipped ("several other effects, very similar to testosterone. I don't want to bother you with that"): more ACTH, well-being, edema, closing the epiphyses, a rise in plasma CBG, TBG, SHBG and transferrin (the opposite of testosterone), potentiation of progesterone, and inhibition of FSH and LH at high concentrations. Therapeutic estrogens The indications: primary hypogonadism in women (as testosterone is used in men), postmenopausal hormone therapy, oral contraceptives, suppressing ovulation in intractable dysmenorrhea or hirsutism, and fertility treatments. Estradiol The main natural estrogen of premenopausal women; a patch (Estraderm), a gel (Estrogel) or a sustained-release intramuscular injection (Depo-Estradiol) Replacement Ethinyl estradiol Semi-synthetic Oral contraceptives Estrone Natural; the main ingredient of conjugated estrogens (Premarin), extracted from pregnant mares Postmenopausal hormone therapy He made the pairing explicit. For hormone therapy in menopause, "that's what Premarin is for. That's estrone, and not estradiol. Ethinyl estradiol, that is for contraception." His figure of estrogen as hormone therapy in menopause sets the good effects against the bad. Good: it strengthens bones, improves cholesterol (lower LDL, higher HDL) and reduces menopausal symptoms such as hot flashes. Bad: it increases the risk of breast cancer, of uterine cancer and of blood clots. The figure's footnote: the added uterine cancer risk can be reduced or eliminated by giving progesterone along with estrogen. The figure says estrogen lowers LDL, while the effects slide says a slight increase in LDL. The point the lecture leans on is HDL: estrogen raises it, testosterone lowers it. Estrogen's adverse effects, contraindications and interactions Common side effects: nausea, fluid retention, breakthrough bleeding, a change in menstrual flow and breast tenderness. Fluid retention is common to both androgens and estrogens, and it worsens hypertension, heart failure and other cardiovascular problems. Serious effects: thromboembolic complications, endometrial carcinoma, breast carcinoma and hypertension. In men, estrogen causes feminization of the genitalia and impotence. "I can't say it enough": clots are very well known with estrogens. Contraindications: pregnancy, incomplete bone growth, undiagnosed genital bleeding, stroke, thrombophlebitis or thromboembolic disease, heart disease, and women with a family history of breast or uterine cancer (the BRCA gene). A history counts however old it is: a heart attack or any clotting event, stroke included, "it doesn't matter, 10 years ago": if you see it in a case, the patient should not take any estrogen product. And a family history counts too: it doesn't have to be the patient herself. Drug interactions: estrogens decrease the efficacy of oral anticoagulants, because they increase the production of clotting factors, and of hypoglycemic agents. His slide writes "thrombolytic complications," and he said it aloud too, but the meaning is clots forming (thrombotic or thromboembolic events), not clots dissolving. SERMs: why a drug can be selective For androgens there were three ways to block them. For estrogen, the main class is the selective estrogen receptor modulators, or SERMs. Estrogen has two receptor subtypes, ER-alpha and ER-beta, and different tissues express them at different levels: differential tissue expression. Binding to DNA and transcription factors also depends on the shape the receptor takes. So one drug can be pro-estrogenic in one tissue, partly estrogenic in another and anti-estrogenic in a third. That is why they are called modulators: an antagonist in one tissue and an agonist in another. Tamoxifen Tamoxifen (Nolvadex) is one of the most popular SERMs, used to treat breast cancer. In the breast it binds the estrogen receptor as an antagonist, so the breast cells stop proliferating, which lowers cancer risk. In the uterus the receptor subtype is different, and tamoxifen activates it: endometrial cells proliferate, and the risk of uterine cancer rises. His figure of tamoxifen's effects: good, it reduces breast cancer risk, lowers LDL and strengthens bones; bad, it increases uterine cancer risk and blood clot risk. Not every breast cancer is fueled by estrogen, so the tumor is tested first. When the cancer cells overexpress estrogen receptors (they are ER-positive), the growth is being fueled by estrogen, and an anti-estrogen will work: "That is the only time you give tamoxifen." His slide: tamoxifen is most effective in ER-positive tumors, with about a 50 percent response. It is not for indiscriminate use in every breast cancer. Raloxifene Raloxifene (Evista), close to tamoxifen, is used mainly to treat osteoporosis in postmenopausal women: it has a preference for the receptors in bone. It has a high affinity for both ER-alpha and ER-beta, and it does not cause proliferation of the endometrium or of breast tumor cells. Its side effect: a 2- to 3-fold increase in the risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Agonist or antagonist, these modulators should be avoided in patients with a history of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism. Clomiphene Clomiphene (Clomid) is used to induce ovulation: "kind of first-line drug for fertility." It is a weak agonist and strong antagonist at the estrogen receptors. By blocking them, it opposes the negative feedback of the body's own estrogen, so the LH and FSH pulses grow larger, and the ovary is driven to ovulate. It works in women whose hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis is intact. Adverse effects: multiple births, because several eggs can be released (twins, triplets, even quadruplets), and ovarian cysts. The SERM summary table His summary table compares each drug with estradiol, tissue by tissue. A plus means the same effect as estrogen, and a minus the opposite effect. Estradiol Inhibits Stimulates Stimulates Promotes Improves Tamoxifen Opposite (doesn't inhibit) Opposite (blocks) Same (stimulates) Same (promotes) Same (improves) Raloxifene Opposite (doesn't inhibit) Opposite (blocks) Opposite (no stimulation) Same (promotes) Same (improves) Clomiphene Opposite (induces it) Opposite Opposite Opposite Opposite How he read it: some, like tamoxifen, stimulate the uterus, and others don't; tamoxifen and raloxifene both act like estrogen on bone; none of them stimulates breast cells; and none of them inhibits ovulation. The same receptors are expressed at different levels in different cells, which is why the drugs have different uses: "So again, tamoxifen for breast cancer, raloxifene for osteoporosis, Clomid, that is for, to stimulate ovulation." The full table also lists toremifene (Fareston) and ospemifene (Osphena), which match tamoxifen; bazedoxifene (Duavee), which matches raloxifene; and fulvestrant (Faslodex), which matches clomiphene. "They are rarely used," he said. Aromatase inhibitors Instead of blocking the estrogen receptor, you can stop estradiol from being made. Testosterone is aromatized to estradiol by aromatase, a natural enzyme, so an aromatase inhibitor inhibits the conversion of testosterone to estradiol. The most popular is anastrozole (Arimidex); letrozole (Femara) and exemestane (Aromasin) are the others. Use: breast cancer treatment. Adverse effects: hot flashes, GI disturbances, CNS disturbances (anxiety, confusion, depression) and thromboembolism. He said these drugs share estrogen-type side effects whether they act for or against estrogen: "At least you should be able to remember hot flashes... and thromboembolism." Contraindications: hepatic damage and premenopausal women. The hot flashes come from the fall in estrogen, the same reason they come at menopause. The slide doesn't say why premenopausal women are excluded; the textbook reason is that before menopause the ovaries make most of the estrogen, and lowering it raises FSH and LH, which drive the ovaries harder. Progesterone Progesterone is made in the adrenal cortex, the corpus luteum, the placenta and the testes. He assumed you know its physiology; the action he stressed is the maturation of the endometrium. His slide lists others he didn't go through: it stimulates lipase, glycogen storage and insulin activity; competitively inhibits mineralocorticoid receptors, so less sodium is reabsorbed; raises body temperature; increases the breathing response to carbon dioxide; drives the alveolobular development of the breast; and increases urinary nitrogen excretion. The progestin drugs The progestins are analogs of progesterone. He highlighted progesterone itself (Prometrium), hydroxyprogesterone and levonorgestrel. The slide also lists medroxyprogesterone (Provera), desogestrel, norgestimate, norethindrone, drospirenone, megestrol (Megace) and dienogest, and two combinations: etonogestrel with ethinyl estradiol (NuvaRing), and medroxyprogesterone with conjugated estrogens (Prempro). Progestins are what we use for contraception, regular and emergency. Many women cannot take estrogen: a family history of thromboembolism, or a history of breast or uterine cancer. If they choose contraception, they have to avoid the pills that contain ethinyl estradiol and take a progestin-only contraceptive. Levonorgestrel is the most common progestin in oral contraceptives, and Plan B, the emergency contraceptive, is just a high strength of levonorgestrel. His Cases 3, 4 and 5 Case 3: in a health-education talk, a teenager asks about combination versus progestin-only contraceptives. Of ethinyl estradiol, estradiol, levonorgestrel and estrone, which has the least estrogenic effect? Levonorgestrel, a progestin; the other three are estrogens. Case 4: a 38-year-old man taking finasteride for androgenic alopecia comes in for a crown and mentions decreased libido and mild breast tenderness. Which enzyme does finasteride inhibit? 5-alpha-reductase, one of the two examples he highlighted: it prevents the conversion of testosterone to its active form. Gynecomastia and sexual dysfunction are the class's side effects. Case 5: a 62-year-old woman with osteoporosis takes raloxifene and comes in because a tooth extraction site is healing slowly. Which added risk, like estrogen therapy's, should the dentist be aware of? Thromboembolic events during immobilization. "Regardless of if they are antagonists or agonists," these drugs share estrogen's side effects. Gingival hyperplasia, immunosuppression and low calcium were the case's wrong choices. The pharmacology of progestins Mechanism: activation of the progestin receptor, which suppresses FSH (and LH and estradiol) secretion, preventing ovulation. Uses: replacement, contraception before and after intercourse (pre- and post-coital), dysmenorrhea, endometriosis, precocious puberty and premenstrual syndrome. Adverse effects: hypertension, lower HDL (an androgenic effect) and cancer risk, especially combined with estrogen. Contraindications: pregnancy desired in the near future, and hypertension. Two slides seem to pull in opposite directions: the hormone therapy figure says adding progesterone lowers estrogen's uterine cancer risk, and the progestin slide lists cancer risk, especially combined with estrogen. Both hold: the progestin protects the endometrium, while combined hormone therapy carries other cancer risk (in standard texts, mainly breast cancer). Anti-progestins and emergency contraception Ulipristal (Ella), the one he highlighted, is a progestin receptor antagonist. Mifepristone (Mifeprex, Korlym) is an antagonist at both the progestin and the glucocorticoid receptors. The slide's use for them: post-coital (emergency) contraception. Contraindications: pregnancy desired in the near future, and Addison disease. Mifepristone blocks cortisol's receptor, and a patient with Addison disease already makes too little cortisol. Emergency contraception, side by side. Plan B is a high dose of levonorgestrel, a progestin; ulipristal is an antagonist: "The difference is this. This is an antagonist." Both have the same indication. The differences he called "probably more important": Plan B has to be used within 72 hours, while ulipristal can be used up to 120 hours, 5 days; and ulipristal is prescription only, while Plan B is sold without a prescription. What it is A high dose of levonorgestrel, a progestin A progestin receptor antagonist Window after intercourse Within 72 hours Up to 120 hours (5 days) Prescription Not needed Needed Summary: the drugs to know His summary slide names the drugs to know in each class: testosterone and DHEA (androgens); finasteride and flutamide (anti-androgens); estradiol, estrone and ethinyl estradiol (estrogens); tamoxifen and raloxifene (SERMs); progesterone and levonorgestrel (progestins); and ulipristal, the emergency contraceptive (anti-progestins). Add the other red drugs: goserelin, dutasteride, bicalutamide, anastrozole and hydroxyprogesterone, with testosterone cypionate and clomiphene, which he stressed aloud. "Pay attention to those drugs that I highlight in the slides, and you should be fine." In the dental chair His two dental cases: a man on finasteride may mention a lower libido or breast tenderness, the side effects of blocking 5-alpha-reductase; and a woman on raloxifene, like a patient on estrogen, carries a higher risk of a clot, especially while she is immobilized after a procedure.
